items.title: Five Steps of Making Human Insulin

source_refs.note: The five steps of making human insulin (PDF 165-166); Figure 20.8 is replaced by the original diagram. The exercises (PDF 166-168) are not part of the lesson body.

items: Preparation of the two genes: because insulin has two distinct chains, two DNA sequences are synthesised, one for chain A and one for chain B.

Construction of recombinant plasmids: the DNA for chain A goes into one set of plasmids and that for chain B into another, often next to a bacterial gene such as lacZ so that the bacteria recognise and express the foreign DNA.
Transformation of host cells: the plasmids are put into two separate cultures of Escherichia coli; culture 1 makes chain A and culture 2 makes chain B.
Fermentation and protein expression: the bacteria are grown in large industrial bioreactors and, as they multiply, read the human DNA and make large amounts of the insulin chains.

Extraction and chemical joining: the bacteria are harvested and the chains extracted and purified; chain A and chain B are mixed and linked by disulfide (sulfur-to-sulfur) bonds between specific amino acids.

blocks.alt: Two parallel rows. Synthetic gene A and synthetic gene B each go into a plasmid beside lacZ, then into its own E. coli culture, then a bioreactor, giving purified chain A and chain B. The chains are mixed and joined by disulfide bridges into human insulin. A box lists the five steps.
blocks.caption: The five steps of making human insulin (original diagram after Figure 20.8).
blocks.long_description: Insulin has two polypeptide chains, so two DNA sequences are synthesised, one for chain A and one for chain B. Each is put into its own set of plasmids, often next to a bacterial gene such as lacZ so that the bacteria recognise and express it. The plasmids are introduced into two separate cultures of Escherichia coli, one making chain A and the other chain B. The bacteria are grown in large industrial bioreactors and make the chains as they multiply. The chains are then extracted and purified, mixed, and linked by disulfide (sulfur-to-sulfur) bonds between specific amino acids, giving functional human insulin identical to that of the pancreas.

blocks.text: This last step gives the functional, three-dimensional human insulin molecule, identical to that made by a healthy human pancreas.

blocks.prompt: Why are chains A and B made in two separate cultures?
blocks.explanation: Each culture carries plasmids with only one of the two genes, so it makes just one chain in large amounts; the purified chains are then joined in the laboratory by disulfide bonds.

items: Two synthetic genes, two plasmid sets, two E. coli cultures.
Bioreactors make the chains; they are purified and joined by disulfide bonds.
